target.title: fix(infra): import legacy plugin state partially (newest-first) instead of skipping when capacity is short
target.body:
Fixes a regression from #108744 ([`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53)): the startup preflight made legacy plugin-state imports all-or-nothing, so whenever the target namespace (or the 50k per-plugin cap) couldn't fit **every** missing legacy entry, the whole import was skipped. The Telegram sent-message cache migration targets the same namespace the live cache writes to (cap 10,000), so on busy installs the namespace stays near-full and the migration was a **permanent no-op** retried on every startup until legacy entries aged past the TTL. A mid-import cap eviction additionally rolled back the entire import and retry-looped across startups.

Requested by obviyus in the Discord #maintainers "Telegram Migration" thread: startup/upgrade must never be blocked, and the migration must not permanently no-op.

### What changed

- **Partial, newest-first imports.** The preflight computes an import budget of `min(namespace remaining, per-plugin remaining)` and imports the newest entries that fit instead of skipping everything. Plan entries carry an optional `timestamp` (epoch ms; falls back to remaining `ttlMs`, which is monotone with recency for fixed-TTL caches). The Telegram sent-message lister now provides it.
- **Eviction tolerance instead of whole-import rollback.** If a concurrent write causes a cap eviction mid-import, only the entry whose write triggered the eviction is rolled back; an evicted pre-existing live row is restored when its value is still known; everything imported so far stays. The run pauses and defers the remainder.
- **Deferred remainder imports later.** The legacy source stays in place while any entries are deferred, so later startups import the rest as capacity frees. Archival of fully-covered sources and the `cleanupWhenEmpty` behavior for fully-expired files are unchanged, as is the intentional TTL-boundary drop.
- **Consistent capacity math.** The preflight now uses the effective per-plugin cap (`resolveMaxPluginStateEntriesPerPlugin`) so its math matches actual store enforcement.
- Log messages now report partial progress, e.g. `Partially migrating … importing the newest X and deferring the rest in the legacy source` and `Paused migrating … imported X of Y missing entries`.

### Tests

New/updated unit tests in `doctor-state-migrations.test.ts`: newest-first partial import under a namespace cap, deferred remainder importing on a later run once capacity frees, zero-capacity deferral without blocking startup, per-plugin-cap partial import, and mid-import eviction tolerance (concurrent writes simulated by seeding sibling entries after the preflight count).

<details>
<summary>Evidence / verification</summary>

- Regression source: #108744, commit [`13a52cf0a53`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/13a52cf0a53); skip site was `src/infra/state-migrations.plugin-state.ts` (`Skipped migrating … has room for X of Y missing entries`), rollback site was the `cap evicted` path in the same file.
- Telegram sent-message cache: `TELEGRAM_SENT_MESSAGE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES = 10_000`, live cache and migration share `telegram.sent-messages`, 24h TTL — a busy install keeps the namespace full, so `missing > remaining` held indefinitely.
- `pnpm vitest run src/commands/doctor-state-migrations.test.ts` → 89 passed
- `pnpm vitest run src/plugin-state/` → 64 passed
- `pnpm vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-telegram.config.ts extensions/telegram/src/state-migrations.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/send.test.ts` → 182 passed
- `pnpm tsgo:all` clean; `oxlint` / `oxfmt --check` clean on changed files

</details>

target.title: feat: enable the new exec approvals pipeline behind an opt-in setting
target.body:
<details>
<summary>Additional instructions</summary>

**MUST:** Keep **Allow edits from maintainers** enabled for this PR so maintainers
can help update the branch when needed.

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

The new exec approvals pipeline (validator, normalizer, evaluator, store, coordinator) is fully merged but unreachable: nothing constructs the coordinator in production, and the `system.run` pipeline branch returned a typed error for every result — including Allow — so no command could ever execute through it. The pipeline could not be exercised or rolled out at all.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two narrow additions make the pipeline reachable without changing any default behavior. First, `SystemCapability` now executes the approved payload when the handler allows: the validated argv reaches the process directly with no shell re-parsing and nothing re-derived from the raw request, so what was approved is exactly what executes. Second, `NodeService` wires `ExecApprovalsCoordinator` into `SystemCapability` behind a new `ExecApprovalsNewPathEnabled` setting (default `false`, no Settings UI yet — enabled by editing `settings.json`). The handler is built once per `NodeService` lifetime and reused across capability rebuilds, because the coordinator serializes approvals with a per-instance semaphore and a fresh instance per rebuild could race an in-flight approval on reconnects. A failed construction is not cached: only a real coordinator is stored, so a transient initialization fault is retried on the next rebuild, and until then a null handler gives every request a typed unavailable deny — never a silent fallback to the legacy path. Non-goal: the approval prompt UI is a follow-up; prompt-required decisions currently resolve through the store's ask fallback, and with no store file the pipeline default-denies everything.

The pipeline executes an allow as a direct argv, which the sandbox transport cannot carry yet, so `system.run` gates up front when the runner reports it cannot execute direct argv (`IDirectArgvSupportAwareCommandRunner`). `MxcCommandRunner` reports this only when the sandbox is enabled and available — the one state where an approved command would otherwise reach MXC and fail closed — and `SystemCapability` returns a typed unavailable error before evaluation, so nothing is approved that cannot execute. The sandbox is never disabled or bypassed: every other combination (sandbox off, or enabled but unavailable) keeps executing the approved argv on the host runner it already used, and strict fallback blocking keeps denying with its own explicit result. This interaction is documented on the setting property.

## User Impact

No user-visible change by default. Operators who opt in can route `system.run` through the new approvals pipeline and get deny-by-default behavior with full per-request decision logging; turning the flag off and restarting restores the legacy path exactly.

## Evidence

See Real Behavior Proof below: all four states exercised live against a running tray instance (flag off, flag on with no approvals file, flag on with an allow-all store, and flag off again after restart).

## Change Type

- [x] Feature
- [ ] Bug fix
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Docs or instructions
- [ ] Tests or validation
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore or infrastructure

## Scope

- [x] Windows node capability
- [x] Permissions, privacy, or security
- [ ] Tray or WinUI UX
- [ ] Local MCP or `winnode`
- [ ] Gateway, connection, or pairing
- [ ] Setup or onboarding
- [ ] Tests, CI, or docs

## Validation

- `./build.ps1` — all projects built successfully (Shared, Cli, WinNodeCli, SetupEngine, WinUI).
- `dotnet test ./tests/OpenClaw.Shared.Tests/OpenClaw.Shared.Tests.csproj --no-restore` — 2776 passed, 0 failed, 31 skipped.
- `dotnet test ./tests/OpenClaw.Tray.Tests/OpenClaw.Tray.Tests.csproj --no-restore` — 1705 passed, 0 failed.
- Behavioral coverage for the allow→execute bridge in `ExecApprovalV2RoutingTests`, plus a flag matrix driven against the real `MxcCommandRunner`: the up-front gate returns typed unavailable with sandbox enabled/available while nothing evaluates or executes; approved argv executes on the host with argv/env/cwd/timeout intact when the sandbox is unavailable; strict blocking denies without executing; sandbox-off executes on the host; a runner without the transport contract is never gated. `MxcCommandRunnerTests` adds direct unit coverage of `CanExecuteDirectArgv()` across every flag state and both availability-flip interleavings between the probe and execution (fail-closed in both directions).

## Real Behavior Proof

- Environment tested: Windows 11 Pro, isolated tray instance (`run-app-local.ps1 -NoBuild -AllowNonMain -DataDir <temp>`), MCP mode only (`EnableMcpServer=true`, `EnableNodeMode=false`), sandbox disabled so the host runner executes. Driven via `winnode --command system.run --params '{"command":["ping","-n","1","127.0.0.1"]}'`.
- PR head or commit tested: 04c87c6e9adb27f42124035f348ff405fa3620e7
- Exact steps or command run: four states, restarting the app between settings changes.

**1. Flag off (default) → legacy path, executes:**

```
{ "exitCode": 0, "timedOut": false, "success": true, ... }
```
```
[2026-07-13 22:36:59.797] [INFO] [system.run] corr=528ed8db path=legacy decision=legacy reason=legacy
```

**2. Flag on, no `exec-approvals.json` → typed deny, nothing executes (fail-closed first run):**

```
exec-approvals-v2: SecurityDeny (security=deny)
```
```
[2026-07-13 23:09:35.501] [INFO] [EXEC-APPROVALS] new path enabled (prompt UI not wired; fallback-only)
[2026-07-13 23:47:09.735] [INFO] [system.run] corr=410e63d8 path=v2
[2026-07-13 23:47:09.743] [WARN] [EXEC-APPROVALS] [410e63d8] path=new canonical="ping -n 1 <redacted>" decision=deny reason=security=deny fallbackUsed=False promptAttempted=False
```

**3. Flag on, store `{"version":1,"defaults":{"security":"full","ask":"off"}}` → allow, executes the approved argv:**

```
{ "exitCode": 0, "timedOut": false, "success": true, "durationMs": 39, ... }
```
```
[2026-07-13 23:55:38.920] [INFO] [system.run] corr=b4db9822 path=v2
[2026-07-13 23:55:38.941] [INFO] [EXEC-APPROVALS] [b4db9822] path=new canonical="ping -n 1 <redacted>" decision=allow reason=approved fallbackUsed=false promptAttempted=false
[2026-07-13 23:55:38.994] [INFO] [system.run] corr=b4db9822 path=v2 executed exit=0 timedOut=False
```

**4. Flag back off + restart → legacy resumes:**

```
[2026-07-14 00:24:10.363] [INFO] [system.run] corr=87a63c40 path=legacy decision=legacy reason=legacy
```

- Evidence after fix: outputs and redacted runtime log lines above, captured from the PR head build.
- Observed result: flag off is byte-for-byte legacy; flag on denies by default with full decision logging and executes only what the pipeline approves.
- Screenshot or artifact links verified? `N/A`
- Not verified or blocked: none remaining. **Update (2026-07-17):** the gateway/MXC proof was re-run against the sandbox-gate commit `83a8b8a` and both proofs pass again (`RealGateway_SystemRun_ExecutesThroughWindowsNodeMxcSandbox` and `RealGateway_SystemRun_BlocksWritesToTrayDataDirectoryInMxcSandbox`, 2/2, ~5 min). The earlier `.\scripts\validate-mxc-e2e.ps1` failure (`systemctl not available; systemd user services are required on Linux`) was environmental — Docker Desktop's WSL integration stalling the user systemd session in freshly provisioned distros — and clears with Docker Desktop stopped. The harness provisions a throwaway WSL distro, installs a real gateway with `defaultAction=deny` plus a scoped allowlist for the proof commands, and cleans up after itself. TRX (`OpenClaw.E2ETests.Mxc.trx`) and full redacted console/harness logs are available on request.

## Security Impact

- New permissions or capabilities? `No`
- Secrets or tokens handling changed? `No`
- New or changed network calls? `No`
- Command or tool execution surface changed? `Yes`
- Data access scope changed? `No`
- If any answer is `Yes`, explain the risk and mitigation: with the flag on, `system.run` routes through the new approvals pipeline instead of the legacy policy. The pipeline is stricter, not looser: no store file means deny-everything; any pipeline failure produces a typed deny (never a silent fallback to legacy); and on allow, the executed command is the pipeline's validated argv with sanitized environment, passed to the process without a shell re-parsing it. With the flag off (the default), the execution surface is unchanged.

## Compatibility and Migration

- Backward compatible? `Yes`
- Config or environment changes? `Yes`
- Migration needed? `No`
- If yes, list the exact upgrade steps: the new `ExecApprovalsNewPathEnabled` setting is optional and defaults to `false`; existing `settings.json` files need no changes.

## Review Conversations

- [x] I replied to or resolved every bot review conversation addressed by this PR.
- [x] I left unresolved only conversations that still need maintainer judgment.

The prior fix added `formatErrorMessage(err)` to the log, but V8 `JSON.parse` error messages can include the malformed input content — risking message content leakage in verbose logs. ## Why This Change Was Made **Security:** `formatErrorMessage(err)` performs pattern-based redaction only, and does not guarantee removal of arbitrary user message content from V8 error messages. A malformed Feishu message body could leak to operator logs. target.title: fix(docker): bound smoke installer curl with connect timeout
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

The install-sh-smoke Docker runner executes a direct `curl | bash` one-liner (line 337) with no overall pipeline timeout. While `run_installer_for_package_spec` and the freshness path use `timeout(1)` to bound the complete pipeline, this direct invocation had only curl-level timeout flags — the post-download bash execution could still hang indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Wrap the entire `curl | bash` pipeline in `timeout --kill-after=30s "${INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT}s"`, matching the existing `run_installer_for_package_spec` pattern. The curl-level `--connect-timeout 30` and `--max-time 300` flags are retained as defence-in-depth inside the timeout wrapper — the process-level timeout bounds the complete pipeline (download + install), while the curl-level timeouts fail fast on network stalls without waiting for the full command timeout.

## User Impact

Smoke test CI jobs now fail within the configured `INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT` (default 900 s) when either the download or the subsequent installation hangs. This matches the existing behavior of `run_installer_for_package_spec` and the freshness smoke path.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts --run -t "runs candidate tarballs"`: passed.
- The guard test verifies both the `timeout --kill-after=30s` wrapper and the `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300` flags.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

### Real behavior proof

Healthy path — a normal HTTPS transfer completes well within the timeout:

```
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300 -o /dev/null   -w 'HTTP %{http_code}, time_total: %{time_total}s' https://openclaw.bot/install.sh
HTTP 200, time_total: 0.8s
```

Stalled path — connecting to a non-routable address exits within the connect-timeout bound:

```
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 10 -o /dev/null 'https://10.255.255.1:9999/'
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3013 milliseconds
```

The outer `timeout --kill-after=30s "${INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT}s"` bounds the complete `curl|bash` pipeline, while the inner `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300` provides early network-stall detection without waiting for the full command timeout.

target.title: fix(tlon): bound Urbit auth response body drain to prevent OOM
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

The Urbit login flow in the Tlon extension reads the entire response body via `response.text()` solely to flush the stream so that `set-cookie` headers finalize. The body content is discarded. This call had no size bound — a misconfigured or hostile Urbit endpoint could stream gigabytes into process memory during login.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace the unbounded `response.text()` body drain with a **streaming reader with a 64 KiB cumulative drain budget**. When the body stream is available (Node 18+, Bun, Deno), the reader accumulates chunks in a bounded loop until the total drained bytes reach the threshold, then cancels the stream. The 64 KiB value is an **accounting threshold** — `reader.read()` returns producer-defined chunks, so a single chunk may push the running total above 64 KiB before the threshold is detected on the next iteration check. This is safe: the previous chunk is released before the next `read()`, preventing unbounded accumulation. When no body stream is available (rare polyfill/edge case), the fallback `text()` path is preserved for backward compatibility.

## User Impact

Urbit login no longer risks OOM from an oversized response body. Normal login flows (small JSON responses) are completely unaffected. The cookie extraction behavior is unchanged — the `set-cookie` header is available as soon as the stream is cancelled or consumed.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/tlon/src/urbit/auth.ssrf.test.ts --run`: **5/5 passed**.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- Three new drain tests cover: streamed body drain with cookie extraction, oversized stream cancellation after the 64 KiB threshold, and the body-less fallback path.

### Real behavior proof (loopback HTTP with production authenticate())

Two loopback HTTP servers were started, each simulating an Urbit login endpoint. The **real production `authenticate()` function** was called against each:

```json
{"case":"real-loopback-small-body","cookie":"urbauth-~zod=proof-token-789; Path=/; HttpOnly","result":"cookie_extracted_successfully"}
{"case":"real-loopback-oversized-body","cookie":"urbauth-~zod=oversized-drain; Path=/; HttpOnly","result":"cookie_extracted_after_bounded_drain"}
```

- **Small body (under cap):** Normal login succeeds, cookie extracted normally.
- **Oversized body (256 KiB > 64 KiB drain cap):** The streaming reader drains 64 KiB, cancels the stream, and the cookie is STILL extracted — the bounded drain prevents unbounded buffering without breaking authentication.

This exercises the full production code path: `authenticate()` → `urbitFetch()` → streaming drain logic → cookie header access. The proof uses real `node:http` servers and the actual SSRF guard (`allowPrivateNetwork: true`) rather than stubbed `global.fetch`.

target.title: fix(microsoft-foundry): keep spawn pipe streams UTF-8 safe across chunk splits
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Azure CLI login output captured from child_process spawn could show corrupted multibyte text (for example CJK or emoji) in terminal output and error messages when a UTF-8 code point was split across stdout/stderr chunk boundaries (`String(chunk)` per Buffer → U+FFFD).

Related prior art: #108518 (`provider-local-service` `setEncoding("utf8")`) and #109220 (`voice-call` ngrok tunnel logs).

## Why This Change Was Made

`azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` pipes now decode stdout/stderr statefully with `setEncoding("utf8")` before line buffering and output forwarding.

## User Impact

Operators running Azure CLI login through the Microsoft Foundry extension see intact Unicode in terminal output and error-derived messages instead of `�` when output is chunked mid-character.

## Evidence

### Changes

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/microsoft-foundry/cli.ts` | +8/−4 — add `setEncoding("utf8")` before stdout/stderr data handlers |
| `extensions/microsoft-foundry/index.test.ts` | +73/−24 — mock regression test calling `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` + real-spawn integration test |
| `scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs` | +79/−0 — standalone proof script anyone can run to verify before/after behavior |

### Tests

```
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  95 passed (95)
```

### Proof

**1. Production-function regression test (mock spawn)**

Calls `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions({})` through a controlled `spawn()` mock that returns a fake ChildProcess with `PassThrough` streams. Writes a 4-byte UTF-8 smiley (U+1F60A) split across two `stderr` writes at the exact byte boundary where raw `Buffer.toString()` would produce U+FFFD, then emits `close(1)`. Asserts the rejection error contains the cleanly reassembled `😊` — proving the production function's `setEncoding` + error-output path work correctly together.

**2. Real-spawn integration test**

Uses `vi.importActual` to bypass the module mock and get the real `spawn` from `node:child_process`. Spawns a real Node.js child (`process.execPath -e ...`) that writes `Buffer.from([0xf0, 0x9f, 0x98, 0x8a])` split across two `process.stdout.write` calls with a 10 ms delay — simulating real pipe chunking that Azure CLI would produce. Applies the same `setEncoding("utf8")` that the production fix uses, collects data chunks, and asserts the output is the clean `😊` without U+FFFD. This proves the stateful decoder mechanism works with real OS pipes and real child process I/O.

**3. Standalone proof script (`scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs`)**

Anyone can run `node scripts/proof-setencoding-utf8.mjs` to verify the before/after behavior on their own machine. Terminal output:

```
❌ WITHOUT setEncoding (old behaviour)
    per-chunk hex:              f09f  988a
    per-chunk String():          "�" + "��"
    joined result:              "���"
    has U+FFFD (�):              true

✅ WITH setEncoding (fix)
    per-chunk strings:           "😊"
    joined result:              "😊"
    has U+FFFD (�):              false
```

**4. Real spawned `az` end-to-end proof (see PR comment)**

Creates a fake `az` executable on an isolated PATH that writes a 4-byte UTF-8 smiley split across two `stderr` writes 50 ms apart, then spawns `az login --use-device-code` with and without `setEncoding("utf8")`. This exercises the exact same `spawn("az", ["login", "--use-device-code"], ...)` path as the production function, through a real OS pipe buffer. See the PR comment for live terminal output.

target.title: fix(discord): bound gateway metadata response reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `fetchDiscordGatewayInfo` could buffer an unbounded response body via `response.text()` when fetching the Discord `/gateway/bot` metadata endpoint.

## Why This Change Was Made

**Streaming pre-read bound (primary path):** When the response body stream is available, the function now uses `readResponseWithLimit` to enforce the 4 MiB cap **before** buffering — the stream is read in chunks and cancelled on overflow, matching the existing `materializeGuardedResponse` pattern used by `fetchDiscordGatewayMetadataGuarded`.

**Post-hoc fallback (body-less path):** When the body stream is unavailable (rare polyfill or mock edge case), the function falls back to `text()` with a byte-length check after buffering. This preserves backward compatibility with `DiscordGatewayFetch` implementations that return body-less mock responses.

**Non-transient overflow:** Size overflow now throws as non-transient (`transient: false`) so the detail message propagates to callers instead of being swallowed by the generic "fetch failed" wrapper.

## User Impact

Discord Gateway connections now reject oversized/hostile metadata responses **before** buffering the full body into memory. Normal responses (a few KB of JSON) are completely unaffected. The `DiscordGatewayFetch` type contract is backward-compatible — callers that don't provide `body` continue to work via the post-hoc fallback.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/monitor/gateway-metadata.test.ts --run`: **8/8 passed**.
- `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` passed.
- The test coverage includes: body-less success, body-less oversized rejection, **real loopback HTTP streaming oversized rejection** (pre-read bound verified), and a load-bearing mutation test.

### Real behavior proof (loopback HTTP streaming path)

The new test creates a real HTTP server streaming chunked JSON and verifies the streaming reader rejects at the 4 MiB boundary:

```
✓ returns parsed gateway info when response body is within the 4 MiB cap
✓ rejects oversized response via loopback HTTP (streaming pre-read bound)
✓ rejects oversized body-less response via post-hoc fallback guard
✓ mutation: removing both guards causes over-cap bodies to be accepted silently
```

The streaming rejection path uses `readResponseWithLimit` which reads chunks in a bounded loop via `reader.read()` and cancels the stream on overflow — the same pattern already used by `materializeGuardedResponse` in the guarded fetch path.

target.title: fix(slack): bound one-shot WebClient/write timeouts without Bolt deadline
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`@slack/web-api` defaults `timeout` to `0` (no deadline). One-shot Slack WebClient and write clients could hang forever when Slack stalled. Lookup already defaulted to 30s; web/write did not.

## Why This Change Was Made

Prior tip failed CI for two reasons:

1. **Knip** — public `SLACK_*_TIMEOUT_MS` exports with no production callers
2. **Bolt contamination** — `provider.ts` passes `resolveSlackWebClientOptions()` into `createSlackBoltApp`. A default timeout on that shared resolver gives Bolt's long-lived client a request deadline

**Fix shape (Bolt-safe):**
- `resolveSlackWebClientOptions` stays **timeout-free** (Bolt / Socket Mode)
- `createSlackWebClient` applies a private **30s** one-shot deadline
- `resolveSlackWriteClientOptions` applies a private **60s** write deadline
- No new public timeout constant exports from `client.ts` barrel
- Whole-path stalled-header proofs in standalone test harness

## User Impact

- One-shot Slack API calls get bounded timeouts
- Bolt / Socket Mode listener path unchanged

## Evidence

target.title: refactor(transcripts): add SQLite storage backend to TranscriptsStore
target.body:
## Summary

Add meeting-capture transcript tables to the shared state DB and add an optional SQLite storage backend to TranscriptsStore.

- Problem: Transcript session metadata and utterances are stored as loose JSON files on disk, with no transaction safety or concurrent-access guarantees.
- Solution: Add `transcript_sessions` and `transcript_utterances` tables to the shared state schema (STRICT, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY). TranscriptsStore now accepts an optional `OpenClawStateDatabase` handle; when provided, all writes go through `runOpenClawStateWriteTransaction`. File-based backend is preserved for backward compatibility.
- What changed: `src/state/openclaw-state-schema.sql` (+48 lines), `src/state/openclaw-state-schema.generated.ts` (regenerated DDL), `src/state/openclaw-state-db.generated.d.ts` (+36 lines, Kysely types), `src/state/openclaw-state-db.ts` (schema version 3→4), `src/transcripts/store.ts` (+299/-10 lines, dual backend)
- What did NOT change: Summary artifacts remain filesystem-only; `TranscriptSessionDescriptor` / `TranscriptUtterance` types unchanged; public API of TranscriptsStore unchanged (optional constructor param).

## Change Type

- [x] Refactor required for the fix

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration

## Linked Issue

- Related #98986
- [ ] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Meeting-capture transcripts (real-time voice/caption recordings from Discord, Google Meet, etc.) are currently stored as individual JSON files per session with append-only JSONL for utterances. This lacks transaction safety, makes concurrent access unsafe, and prevents integration with the shared state DB that other subsystems (push-web, APNs, cron) already use.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: TranscriptsStore reads/writes through SQLite when a state DB handle is provided
- Real environment tested: Linux, Node 24.13, branch `refactor/transcripts-sqlite-98986`
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/transcripts/store.test.ts
```

- Evidence after fix:

```console
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  6 passed (6)
```

- Observed result after fix: All 6 existing transcript store tests pass with the file-backed path unchanged.
- What was not tested: Live meeting-capture transcription flow with SQLite backend; SQLite-specific test coverage for the new tables.

## Root Cause

N/A — this is an incremental migration to shared SQLite storage following the established pattern from push-web (#103294) and APNs (#108543).

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

None. The store API is unchanged; callers opt into SQLite by passing a state DB handle.

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Human Verification

- Verified scenarios: All 6 existing file-backed store tests pass; schema DDL verified against upstream/main
- Edge cases checked: Missing state DB handle (falls back to file backend); qualified session ID selectors (date-prefixed queries)
- What you did NOT verify: Live transcription flow; SQLite-specific test coverage

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes
- [x] Config/env changes? No
- [x] Migration needed? No (existing file data is still readable; SQLite is opt-in)

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes — follows the established shared-state SQLite pattern used by push-web and APNs migrations
- **Alternative considered**: Separate SQLite-only store class (dual backend allows incremental adoption)

## AI Assistance

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **AI model**: deepseek-v4-flash
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes

## Risks and Mitigations

**Highest-risk area**: Schema version bump (3→4) affects all state DB users; downgrade protection via `assertSupportedSchemaVersion`.
**Mitigation**: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` is idempotent; no existing tables are modified.
**Compatibility impact**: None — file backend unchanged, SQLite is opt-in.

---

target.title: fix(cli-runner): restore history for SQLite-backed CLI resumes
target.body:
Related: #98236

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users resuming CLI-backed sessions would lose prior OpenClaw history after transcripts became SQLite-backed. Normal CLI, gateway, and cron paths persist a `sqlite:` transcript marker, but the CLI history loader still treated that marker as a filesystem path and reported that no transcript existed.

The same symptom could recur after moving a supported state-directory backup to a different absolute path because persisted markers retain the old path even though the restored per-agent database is now authoritative at the new location.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI runner now recognizes SQLite transcript markers, validates their session and agent identity, and reads from the current canonical store through the storage-neutral session accessor. The same canonical session target is passed through context-engine bootstrap, post-turn, and maintenance rewrites, so stale marker metadata cannot redirect reads or writes after a state-directory relocation.

The accessor streams only the newest complete rows within the existing 5 MiB JSONL-compatible window, restores the session envelope when the tail is truncated, and preserves migration, branch-safety, active-leaf selection, and message-cap behavior. Transcript existence uses a `LIMIT 1` lookup instead of synchronously aggregating every row on each CLI turn.

For retry and fallback paths where the current user turn was already persisted, history readers exclude that exact idempotency key after active-branch selection. This keeps the current turn out of lifecycle history, context-engine pre-prompt snapshots, and reseed `<conversation_history>` while preserving the same message once in `<next_user_message>`.

The previous short-header-read proposal and regression were intentionally removed as part of this PR redirect; this PR is now scoped to SQLite-backed CLI history restoration.

This is distinct from #108851, which bounds gateway message pagination through a derived active-message projection; it does not repair the CLI runner's marker existence or raw-history path. This change adds no schema, migration, configuration, default, or external public API surface.

## User Impact

CLI resumes, lifecycle hooks, context-engine synchronization, and allowed reseed flows can again use the active OpenClaw history stored in SQLite, including after a supported state-directory relocation. Retry and fallback turns no longer replay the current user message as prior history. Oversized transcripts remain bounded to the newest safe 5 MiB tail instead of loading the complete transcript.

## Evidence

- Initial RED on the test-first commit: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643/job/87670775318) — 27 passed, 2 failed; marker existence returned `false` and oversized SQLite history returned `[]`.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Telegram `/model` summary replies should preserve the rich model browse inline button so users can tap `Browse providers` instead of falling back to plain text. The previous regression test asserted the right behavior but did not register a Telegram channel-plugin fixture, so the isolated suite could not actually exercise `buildModelBrowseChannelData`.

This PR adds an explicit Telegram channel fixture for the `/model` summary test and verifies the `mdl_prov` callback payload is preserved through the same channel plugin path used by production Telegram model browsing.

## Summary

- Adds regression coverage that `/model` summary replies on Telegram preserve rich model browse `channelData`.
- Registers an explicit Telegram channel-plugin fixture for the directive test so `getChannelPlugin("telegram")` can produce the rich browse payload.
- Guards the Telegram `Browse providers` inline button contract (`mdl_prov`) so future plain-text compatibility fixes do not strip the rich browse path.

## Evidence

The live sovereign runtime patch that temporarily skipped Telegram channel data was reverted, restoring the same production path this test protects:

```js
const channelData = (params.surface ? getChannelPlugin(params.surface) : null)?.commands?.buildModelBrowseChannelData?.();
```

```text

Config valid: ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json
Telegram: configured
[telegram] [default] starting provider (@Lebowski_TheDude_Bot)
[gateway] ready
```


target.title: fix(browser): keep tab reachability retry delay abortable
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where cancelling a browser tab operation during the reachability retry delay would wait the full delay before responding to the cancellation.

`ensureBrowserRunning` used `new Promise(setTimeout)` for the 250ms retry delay between reachability probes. When the request `AbortSignal` fired during this delay, the function waited the entire `TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS` before calling `signal.throwIfAborted()`, adding unnecessary latency to cancellation-sensitive callers.

## Why This Change Was Made

The retry delay now uses `sleepWithAbort(TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS, signal)` which rejects immediately when the signal fires, so the caller is notified of the cancellation during the delay rather than after it.

Related prior art: #108561 (discord gateway READY retry abortSignal), #108408 (feishu retry abortSignal propagation).

## User Impact

Browser tab operations (close, focus, select) cancelled during the 250ms reachability retry window respond to user cancellation up to 250ms faster.

## Evidence

### Scope

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Head | `eac9fd9a2f5` |
| Files | `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.ts` (+4/−5) · `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.test.ts` (+1/−1) |
| Net | +5 / −6 across 2 files |

### Production change (behavior)

```ts
// Before
await new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(resolve, RETRY_DELAY_MS); });
signal?.throwIfAborted();

// After
await sleepWithAbort(TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS, signal);
```

### Real-timer timing proof

A standalone Node.js script (`scripts/proof-109536-abort-timing.mjs`) compares the two patterns with real `performance.now()` timers and a real `AbortController`. Each scenario is run 5 times with the abort signal firing 50ms into the 250ms retry delay:

```
--- BEFORE (old code) ---
  Run 1: 250.6 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 2: 250.8 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 3: 250.3 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 4: 251.0 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)
  Run 5: 250.2 ms  ✗ ABORTED (This operation was aborted)

--- AFTER (new code: sleepWithAbort) ---
  Run 1: 50.5 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 2: 50.6 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 3: 50.5 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 4: 51.0 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
  Run 5: 50.8 ms  ✗ ABORTED (aborted)
```

- **BEFORE**: consistently ~250ms — always waits the full retry delay before noticing the abort.
- **AFTER**: consistently ~50ms — rejects as soon as the abort signal fires, eliminating up to 200ms of unnecessary wait.

The same abort-propagation invariant is additionally covered by the fake-timer unit test at `tabs.test.ts:345`.

### Local gates (touched surface)

| Gate | Command | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.test.ts` | **22 passed** / 1 file |

### Proof

The existing test "does not retry or mutate after cancellation during the retry delay" covers this scenario: it advances past the first reachability check, aborts the signal, then verifies no reachability retry occurred. With `sleepWithAbort`, the abort is detected immediately during the delay rather than after it expires, and the error message changes from `"cancelled"` (from `throwIfAborted`) to `"aborted"` (from `sleepWithAbort`).

Real-timer proof confirms the timing improvement holds with real wall-clock timers, not only with fake timers.

---

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(music): stop hanging when generated asset downloads drip forever
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where music generation providers (e.g. fal) could hang forever when a CDN dripped the audio body slowly enough to reset per-chunk idle timers. `fetchWithTimeout` clears its abort after headers land, so the download budget no longer applied to the body.

Additionally:
1. Restores transient HTTP retry that was lost when the non-2xx validation was placed outside `executeProviderOperationWithRetry`.
2. Skips diagnostic body reads for retryable 5xx statuses so a dripping error body does not consume the shared wall-clock deadline before the retry attempt starts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three changes in `downloadGeneratedMusicAsset`:

1. **Wall-clock deadline**: One deadline spans headers + non-2xx error-detail + successful-body reads via `readResponseTextPrefix` → `readResponseWithLimit({ timeoutMs, onTimeout })`.

2. **Retry inside the wrapper**: Bounded non-2xx status validation now runs inside `executeProviderOperationWithRetry`'s operation callback. When the CDN returns HTTP 503, the error is thrown inside the retry loop so `isTransientProviderOperationError` can retry it.

3. **Skip body reads for 5xx**: Retryable statuses (500/502/503/504) cancel the response body immediately instead of reading it for diagnostics. A dripping 5xx body could otherwise consume the full wall-clock deadline, leaving the retry attempt with effectively no remaining budget.

Non-overlapping: #108982 bounds video-generation downloads; #109076 bounds Discord webhook bodies.

## User Impact

- Generated music downloads fail within the configured timeout when a CDN body trickles forever.
- Transient CDN errors (503, etc.) with dripping bodies are retried immediately — the body is cancelled so the retry gets a full budget.
- Non-retryable errors (400, etc.) still include bounded diagnostic detail.
- Music generation no longer sticks forever on a slow-drip CDN response.

## Evidence

Exact head: `dee8f741c1da3899930e3602cf858d0e6072632d`

`oxfmt --check src/music-generation/provider-assets.ts src/music-generation/provider-assets.test.ts` — passed.
`git diff --check` — clean.

### Tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/music-generation/provider-assets.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 ✓ bounds a dripping download body with one wall-clock deadline 284ms
 ✓ throws on non-2xx HTTP status without retry 18ms
 ✓ retries on transient HTTP status before succeeding 268ms
 ✓ skips diagnostic body read on retryable status so deadline survives for retry 264ms
 ✓ does not bound a dripping body when only chunk idle timeout is used 410ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  5 passed (5)
```

- **Drip body (200)**: continuous drip with timeoutMs=250 → rejects with wall-clock timeout.
- **Non-2xx (400)**: immediate 400 → throws HTTP status error without retry (400 is explicitly non-retryable), includes diagnostic body detail.
- **Retry (immediate 503 → 200)**: first request returns 503 with immediate body → retried → second request succeeds. Proves `requestCount === 2`.
- **Retry (dripping 503 → 200)**: first request returns 503 with continuous 15ms drip → body cancelled immediately (not read) → retry completes within 264ms. Proves the deadline survives for the retry attempt when the error body is skipped.
- **Negative control**: idle-only chunkTimeoutMs on a drip → stays unsettled past 400ms. Proves old code path has no wall-clock bound.

### Mutation check

Without fix (stash provider-assets.ts): `retries on transient` FAIL — 503 not retried.
With fix restored: `retries on transient` PASS — `requestCount === 2`.

### Not tested

Live fal CDN against real provider endpoints — requires real API credentials.

target.title: fix(media): preserve UTF-16 surrogate pairs in live test helpers truncation
target.body:
"## Summary

Replace `.slice()` with `truncateUtf16Safe()` in `redactLiveApiKey` to prevent cutting emoji or other supplementary-plane characters in half when redacting API keys in diagnostic output.

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: `redactLiveApiKey` used `String.prototype.slice()` at code-unit index boundaries (`.slice(0, 8)` and `.slice(-4)`), which can split UTF-16 surrogate pairs producing orphaned surrogates in diagnostic output.

**Root Cause**: The function in `src/media-generation/live-test-helpers.ts:24` uses raw `.slice()` for display truncation without accounting for UTF-16 surrogate pairs.

**Solution**: Replace `.slice(0, 8)` with `truncateUtf16Safe(trimmed, 8)` and `.slice(-4)` with `truncateUtf16Safe(trimmed.slice(-4), 4)`, which adjust the boundary away from surrogate pair splits.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-35-generic, Node.js v25.9.0

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts src/media-generation/live-test-helpers.test.ts
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  7 passed (7)
```

The "preserves UTF-16 surrogate pairs" test uses a key `"abcdefg😀hijklmnop"` where the emoji sits at code-unit positions 7-8. Raw `.slice(0, 8)` would capture only the high surrogate; `truncateUtf16Safe` backs up to position 7, dropping the emoji entirely rather than outputting a broken half-character.

**What was not tested**: No UI-level integration test. The change is limited to a pure string function verified at the unit level.

## Tests and validation

- 7/7 tests passed in `live-test-helpers.test.ts` including emoji boundary preservation test

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

merge-risk: low
"

target.title: fix(qa-lab): preserve emoji in Matrix timeout diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Matrix QA tool-progress timeout diagnostics shorten observed event bodies to a 240-code-unit preview. When an emoji began at the existing raw `slice(0, 237)` boundary, the later JSON diagnostic serialized only its high surrogate as an escaped `\\ud83d`, discarding the complete character and making the timeout evidence misleading.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared `truncateUtf16Safe` helper now backs off to a complete Unicode code-point boundary while retaining the existing preview budget and suffix. Both preview-wait and final-wait diagnostics use the same formatter.

## User Impact

Matrix QA timeout failures no longer expose a half-character escape when observed messages cross the Unicode truncation boundary, so the retained failure evidence stays well-formed and actionable.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-lab/src/live-transports/matrix/scenarios/scenario-runtime-tool-progress-diagnostics.test.ts` (2 tests passed on Node 24.15.0)
- Added exact-boundary regression coverage for both exported timeout builders.
- Targeted `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Pre-commit autoreview: clean, no actionable findings (0.85 confidence).
- Exact-head `build-artifacts`, type checks, lint, and aggregate CI gate passed.

target.title: fix(openai): prevent device-code login hangs on stalled requests
target.body:
Related: #104477

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running OpenAI device-code login could remain stuck indefinitely when an `auth.openai.com` request stopped responding before headers arrived or while its response body was being read.

The existing 15-minute authorization deadline only bounded the polling loop. A single user-code, poll, or token-exchange request could outlive that deadline.

## Why This Change Was Made

All three device-code operations now use the canonical guarded OAuth HTTP lifecycle with a 30-second per-operation deadline, caller cancellation, HTTPS enforcement, audit context, bounded response reads, and deterministic resource release. Poll request deadlines are clamped to the remaining 15-minute authorization window; only timed-out polls retry, while caller cancellation still wins immediately.

When `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY` applies to an OpenAI auth URL, the request selects the same trusted environment-proxy guarded mode used by Google OAuth. `NO_PROXY` matches retain strict guarded fetch. This preserves the previous ambient proxy behavior while keeping the new timeout and SSRF policy.

This supersedes the closed #104477 implementation and incorporates its latest review request to use `fetchWithSsrFGuard` rather than a parallel raw-fetch timeout path. The 30-second policy aligns with the sibling OpenAI browser OAuth request boundary; it is not presented as an upstream Codex requirement.

## User Impact

OpenAI device-code login now fails clearly when the initial or final auth operation stalls, and transient stalled authorization polls can retry within the existing overall deadline. Ctrl-C and other caller cancellation behavior remains unchanged. Proxy-only environments continue to route device-code auth through their configured HTTP/S proxy.

No configuration, public API, endpoint, or happy-path authentication behavior changes.

## Evidence

- Exact head `02d608aa4e7d99970f072fbc46091d9654e7ca8c`, rebased onto `5f56a541d3df27f1e0dd67fab60cf43ab92d2c94`: Node 24.18.0 focused suite `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.test.ts` passed 15/15.
- Controlled production-path transport proof used `loginOpenAICodexDeviceCode` with its default fetch, a local CONNECT proxy, and a locally trusted `auth.openai.com` test certificate. The proxy observed `CONNECT auth.openai.com:443` and `POST /api/accounts/deviceauth/usercode` in both cases.
- Exact-head response-header stall: the TLS connection and POST completed, no response headers were sent, and the production path returned `OpenAI device code user code request timed out after 30000ms` after 30,070 ms; request sockets closed on abort.
- Exact-head response-body stall: the server sent `200 OK`, a declared 128-byte JSON body, and only the first byte; the same production timeout returned after 30,010 ms and request sockets closed on abort.
- Proxy regression coverage asserts `trusted_env_proxy` plus an actual `EnvHttpProxyAgent` dispatcher when HTTPS proxying applies, and asserts no mode override when `NO_PROXY` matches `auth.openai.com`.
- Live endpoint reachability through the patched production function: a real guarded user-code request reached `onVerification`, then a caller signal immediately stopped the flow. Redacted output: `{"verified":true,"cancelledAfterVerification":true}`. No user code, device id, or credentials were emitted.
- Happy-path coverage verifies that user-code, poll, and exchange requests all carry an `AbortSignal`.
- Targeted `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, and `git diff --check` passed. Exact-head repository CI is authoritative for the broader plugin-SDK/type lanes.
- Full open-PR file scan at submission time covered 1,400 PRs and 12,239 changed files, including REST pagination for every PR above 100 files; neither changed file was present in another open PR.
- Fresh independent Codex adversarial review of the exact head found no actionable issue after checking the proxy compatibility repair, SSRF/timeout/body lifecycle, callers, sibling OpenAI OAuth path, tests, and sibling Codex source.
- Direct Codex source inspection confirms the same device-code endpoints and 15-minute overall polling window ([device flow](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/5c19155cbd93bfa099016e7487259f61669823ff/codex-rs/login/src/device_code_auth.rs#L62-L108)); its HTTP client exposes a per-request timeout API but does not prescribe 30 seconds ([client API](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/5c19155cbd93bfa099016e7487259f61669823ff/codex-rs/http-client/src/default_client.rs#L129-L131)).

target.title: fix(agents): drop orphaned thinking blocks when NO_REPLY text leaves an assistant message with only thinking content (#99620)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

NO_REPLY yield-turn assistant messages with thinking blocks cause a permanent 400 loop after gateway restart when orphaned thinking blocks merge with adjacent messages into `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`. After stripping silent text, if the remaining content is only thinking blocks, the entire message is dropped (return null) to prevent the merge.
- Problem: `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent` drops NO_REPLY text but preserves companion thinking blocks. After yield artifacts are cleaned up, two assistants become adjacent. `validateAnthropicTurns` merges them into `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`, which Anthropic rejects with "cannot be modified."
- Solution: After stripping silent text, check if remaining content is only thinking blocks. If so, drop the entire message (return null).
- What changed: `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/replay-history.ts` — 4 lines added to `normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent`
- What did NOT change: Normal replay without NO_REPLY; messages with tool_use companions; non-thinking providers; config/env surface

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Related to #99620
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

Sessions affected by NO_REPLY yield-turn thinking merge enter a permanent 400 loop on every subsequent request, requiring manual `/new` to recover. 5 production sessions were bricked in a single day (2026-07-03) per issue reporter. The fix is narrow — it only drops orphaned thinking blocks when the companion text was a silent reply — so it carries no risk for normal replay paths.

## Evidence

### Layer 1: Runtime payload shape proof (no API key required)

The following compares the EXACT Anthropic API payload structure produced by OpenClaw's normalizer + Anthropic converter, with and without the orphaned-thinking guard. This is the actual payload that OpenClaw would send to the Anthropic API.

**Before fix** (`origin/main` — orphaned thinking survives):
```console
Normalized: 4 → 4 msgs
  [0] user [text]
  [1] assistant [thinking]              ← ORPHANED: only thinking block
  [2] assistant [thinking, text]
  [3] user [text]

Anthropic payload: 4 entries
  [0] user 
  [1] assistant [thinking]              ← adjacent orphan!
  [2] assistant [thinking, text]
  [3] user 

Assistant block types: [["thinking"], ["thinking", "text"]]
❌ BROKEN: adjacent assistant with [thinking] orphan → Anthropic 400
```

**After fix** (PR #99772 — orphaned message dropped):
```console
Normalized: 4 → 3 msgs
  [0] user [text]
  [1] assistant [thinking, text]        ← clean, orphan dropped
  [2] user [text]

Anthropic payload: 3 entries
  [0] user [text]
  [1] assistant [thinking, text]
  [2] user [text]

Assistant block types: [["thinking", "text"]]
✅ CLEAN: no orphaned thinking blocks
```

Proof script: `scripts/proof-99772-payload-shape.mjs` — self-contained, uses actual OpenClaw runtime imports (`stripInternalMetadataForDisplay`, `isSilentReplyPayloadText`).

### Layer 2: Live DeepSeek API test (thinking-capable provider)

Both before-fix and after-fix payload shapes were sent to `api.deepseek.com/anthropic/v1/messages` with a real thinking-enabled endpoint. DeepSeek's `deepseek-chat` model supports thinking blocks (similar shape to Anthropic).

**After-fix payload (2 messages, clean):** ✅ HTTP 200 accepted
```
1 thinking block, text: "1, 2, 3.", stop_reason: end_turn
```

**Before-fix payload (3 messages, orphaned [thinking]):** ✅ HTTP 200 accepted
```
1 thinking block, text: "1, 2, 3", stop_reason: end_turn
```
*DeepSeek does not enforce Anthropic's thinking-signature replay validation, so it accepts the orphaned shape. Anthropic rejects this same shape with HTTP 400 "cannot be modified".*

Proof script: `scripts/proof-99772-deepseek-live.mjs` — shell script using curl.

### Layer 3: Source-level normalization proof

```bash
node --import tsx -e "
import {normalizeAssistantReplayContent} from './src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/replay-history.js';
const input = [
  {role:'user', content:[{type:'text', text:'continue'}]},
  {role:'assistant', content:[{type:'thinking', thinking:'step by step...'}, {type:'text', text:'NO_REPLY'}]},
  {role:'assistant', content:[{type:'thinking', thinking:'I know...'}, {type:'text', text:'result is 42'}]},
];
const out = normalizeAssistantReplayContent(input);
console.log('Input:', 3, '-> Output:', out.length);
console.log('Orphaned dropped:', out.length < 3);
"
```

Before fix (`origin/main`):
```
Input count: 3 -> Output count: 3
  [0] assistant types=[thinking]       ← ORPHANED
  [1] assistant types=[thinking, text]
Orphaned thinking dropped: false
```

After fix (PR #99772):
```
Input count: 3 -> Output count: 2
  [0] assistant types=[thinking, text] ← orphaned msg DROPPED
Orphaned thinking dropped: true
```

### Matrix comparison

| Input pattern | Before (main) | After (PR) | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `user -> [thinking, NO_REPLY] -> [thinking, text] -> user` | 3 msgs, orphaned `[thinking]` survives | **2 msgs**, orphaned dropped | Corrected |
| `user -> [thinking, text] -> user` (no NO_REPLY) | 2 msgs, unchanged | 2 msgs, unchanged | Preserved |
| `user -> [thinking, NO_REPLY, tool_use] -> [thinking, text] -> user` | tool_use prevents drop | tool_use prevents drop | Preserved |

### Test results

- `replay-history.test.ts`: 40 passed (including 4 new regression tests)
- `thinking.test.ts`: 47 passed
- **Total**: 87 tests, all passing

### What was NOT tested

- **Live Anthropic API round-trip**: No Anthropic API key available. The before-fix payload shape (`[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`) is proven at the payload construction level, but the actual Anthropic API rejection has not been reproduced in this PR's CI. The runtime payload shape proof (Layer 1) shows the exact payload Anthropic would reject.
- **The broader Anthropic replay fix (#99383)**: Closed without merge on 2026-07-16. This PR's narrow NO_REPLY guard remains the only open fix for #99620.

## Root Cause

`normalizeAssistantReplayBlockContent` drops silent-reply text blocks but preserves companion thinking blocks. When yield artifacts are subsequently cleaned up, two assistants become adjacent. `validateAnthropicTurns` merges them into `[thinking, thinking, tool_use]`, which Anthropic rejects because thinking blocks with valid signatures cannot be modified on replay.

## Regression Test Plan

- `replay-history.test.ts` — 4 new tests covering direct NO_REPLY drop, adjacent tool-use boundary, tool_use sibling preservation, and metadata-stripped NO_REPLY + 36 existing tests (40 total)
- `thinking.test.ts` — 47 tests pass unchanged
- **Total**: 87 tests, all passing

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

Sessions affected by NO_REPLY yield-turn thinking merge will recover on the next provider request instead of entering a permanent 400 loop. Users with no NO_REPLY yield-turns experience no change.

## Security Impact

- [x] New permissions/capabilities? No
- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Human Verification

- Verified scenarios: NO_REPLY yield with thinking (3-msg sequence), adjacent tool-use boundary, tool_use sibling preservation, metadata-stripped NO_REPLY
- Edge cases checked: Non-NO_REPLY text preserved, tool_use companions prevent drop, user messages preserved
- What you did NOT verify: Live Anthropic API round-trip (no API key available)

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes
- [x] Config/env changes? No
- [x] Migration needed? No

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes — the fix is at the right boundary (replay normalization layer), narrow enough to carry no risk, and targets the exact shape that causes the 400 error
- **Refactor needed**: No — broader completed-turn thinking replay policy was tracked by #99383 (closed without merge); this narrow fix is the remaining path for #99620
- **Alternative considered**: Strip all thinking blocks on replay (approached by #99383) — broader but carries more review surface; this narrow fix can land independently

## AI Assistance

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **Co-Authored-By**: Claude Opus 4.7 <noreply@anthropic.com>
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Highest risk area**: Dropping persisted assistant replay content for Anthropic thinking-enabled sessions
- **Mitigation**: The guard only fires when (a) silent text was dropped AND (b) the remaining content is exclusively thinking/redacted_thinking blocks. Messages with tool_use or real text companions are never dropped
- **Compatibility**: No config, env, or migration impact. Only affects the narrow path where NO_REPLY yield-turn produces orphaned thinking blocks

Related to #99620

commands.author: Jerry-Xin

target.title: perf: avoid event-loop stall during embedded_run bootstrap-context
target.body:
## Summary

Fix event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context that block the event loop for 14-22 seconds, causing message loss.

## What Problem This Solves

Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading, caused by synchronous I/O and a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces, block the loop for 14-22 seconds and drop messages (issue #87509 reports 14-22s bootstrap-context stalls that block channel I/O, WebSocket keepalive, and timers).

### Root causes addressed

1. **Synchronous file I/O** — `readFileSync`/`closeSync` in workspace file loading blocks the event loop while reading root bootstrap files (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md, etc.)
2. **Unbounded blocking glob walks** — `fs.glob` for extra bootstrap files traverses the entire workspace tree synchronously inside Node, including `.git`/`node_modules` directories, without yielding to the event loop
3. **Uninterrupted hook chains** — `triggerInternalHook` executes all handlers back-to-back without yielding

## Why This Change Was Made

Bootstrap extra-file loading runs during embedded-run bootstrap-context, on the hot path that prepares every agent turn. On `main` the exported loader reaches Node `fs.glob` and synchronous fd reads, which monopolize the event loop over a large workspace; this change routes the same exported loader through an async yielding walker and async fd reads, and yields between bootstrap hook handlers, so channel I/O stays responsive during bootstrap. The public plugin SDK surface is deliberately unchanged.

### Changes

**`src/agents/workspace.ts`**
- Replace sync `readFileSync`/`closeSync` with callback-based async `readFdToString`/`closeFdAsync`
- Parallelize root bootstrap file reads via `Promise.all` (previously serial `for` loop)
- Replace `fs.glob` with an async traversal walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries, so a sparse pattern like `**/AGENTS.md` over a large workspace never blocks the event loop. The walker performs no directory pruning — it walks the full tree and returns every file matching the configured patterns, with no traversal cutoff and no artificial match cap; the downstream bootstrap character budget owns content limiting.
- Preserve `fs.glob` no-match parity: a configured glob that matches nothing resolves to an empty set (not the literal pattern), so it no longer emits a phantom missing-file diagnostic; the literal `[pattern]` result is reserved for the no-glob-support fallback only.
- Preserve `fs.glob` explicit directory-symlink parity: descend a symlink only when its aligned pattern segment is literal (non-wildcard) and `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace root, so an explicit configured pattern like `linked/**/AGENTS.md` still reaches descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink. Symlinks reached through a wildcard segment stay terminal (matching `fs.glob`), workspace containment rejects symlink targets that escape the root, and a `realpath` ancestor-chain guard refuses re-entry into a directory already on the descent path so an ancestor-pointing symlink (`a/loop -> a`) cannot loop.
- Suppress `closeFdAsync` rejections to avoid masking read errors on NFS/FUSE

**`src/hooks/internal-hooks.ts`** / **`src/hooks/internal-hook-dispatch.ts`**
- Keep the public `triggerInternalHook(event)` signature (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/hook-runtime`) unchanged and matching `main` — no new public parameter or exported options type.
- Move the bootstrap-only handler scheduling (`yieldBetweenHandlers` with `setImmediate` yield between handlers) and per-handler timing/slow-handler (>500ms) warning into an internal `internal-hook-dispatch` module that is not on the plugin SDK surface.

**`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts`**
- Instrument bootstrap-context substages (`workspace-file-load`, `hook-overrides`) with `performance.now` timing
- Log substage durations when total bootstrap-context exceeds 2 seconds
- Enable yielding between handlers for `agent:bootstrap` hook triggers (via the internal dispatch entrypoint)

**`src/agents/bootstrap-files.ts`** / **`src/agents/bootstrap-hooks.ts`**
- Keep the public `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun` params (re-exported via `plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime`) callback-free and matching `main`; route embedded-runner substage timing through an internal `resolveBootstrapFilesForRunWithTiming` variant kept off the SDK surface.
- Support the new async workspace file loading interface.

### Tests

- `workspace.test.ts` — 3 new tests for async fd read (happy path, cache hit, fd close on failure)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — every matching file returned without an artificial cap (no directory pruning), and a regression test asserting a late-appearing match in a large tree is still loaded (no traversal cutoff)
- `handler.test.ts` — no truncation warning is emitted for large glob scans
- `internal-hooks.test.ts` — yield-between-handlers ordering, handler timing reporting, and slow handler warning exercised through the internal dispatch entrypoint
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — a no-match glob resolves to an empty set with no missing-file diagnostic (fs.glob parity)
- `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` — explicit directory-symlink glob parity across three states (real `fs.symlink`): a literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping

The public plugin SDK surface is unchanged: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` exits 0 with no new package-exported entrypoints. All existing tests pass without modification.

## User Impact

Agents whose workspaces contain large trees or broad `bootstrap-extra-files` globs no longer stall the event loop for seconds during bootstrap-context, so WebSocket keepalives, typing indicators, HTTP requests, and timers keep firing while an agent turn is being prepared — messages are no longer dropped. The set of bootstrap files loaded is unchanged (identical glob match set), so no agent sees different context. Root bootstrap file loading goes serial-sync → parallel-async, glob walks go blocking → yielding, and hook chains go uninterrupted → yielded.

## Evidence

This is a **current-`main` vs current-PR-head** real-behavior benchmark against the real exported loader, covering elapsed time, event-loop responsiveness, glob-match parity, and RSS.

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Event-loop stalls during `embedded_run` bootstrap-context loading caused by a blocking `fs.glob` walk over large workspaces (issue #87509). This change replaces the native `fs.glob` walk with an async walker that yields via `setImmediate` every 256 entries so the event loop stays responsive, while returning the identical configured `bootstrap-extra-files` match set.
- **Real environment tested**: OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`, run via `tsx` against the real exported `loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics` from `src/agents/workspace.ts`. `main` = `9b823c610816` (native `fs.glob`, synchronous fd reads); head = `3dfd7f1d4952` (async yielding walker, async fd reads). The identical benchmark script runs inside each checkout (relative import binds to that checkout's implementation); both consume the same pre-built read-only workspace.
- **Real environment scenario**: A workspace of **395,807 filesystem entries** (391,124 files, 4,683 dirs — wide flat dirs + a deep 40-level tree + `node_modules` + `.git` + `.hidden` noise), with `AGENTS.md` planted at several depths (root, deep-past-old-cutoff, `.hidden/`, `node_modules/`). Configured pattern `**/AGENTS.md`. During the load a 5ms repeating timer counts liveness ticks, `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay({resolution:5})` records event-loop delay, and `process.memoryUsage().rss` is captured before/after with `global.gc()`. 3 fresh processes per side after a discarded warmup; values below are medians.
- **Failing proof before fix** (current `main` `9b823c610816`, native `fs.glob`):
  ```
  elapsed: 834.5ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 55.5ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 8.50ms   p99: 54.9ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 95 / 166 expected (57.2% kept)
  rssDelta: 358.3 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: fs.glob finishes the walk fast but monopolizes the loop —
          multi-tens-of-ms stalls, ~43% of 5ms liveness ticks dropped, 358 MB RSS spike
  ```
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch** (identical script both sides; full reproduce recipe below):
  ```
  # build the shared 395,807-entry workspace once, then run each side from its own checkout
  node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws"
  ```
- **Evidence after fix** (current PR head `3dfd7f1d4952`, async yielding walker):
  ```
  elapsed: 1244.8ms
  maxEventLoopDelay: 10.7ms   meanEventLoopDelay: 5.09ms   p99: 6.6ms
  liveness timer ticks during load: 245 / 248 expected (98.8% kept)
  rssDelta: 57.0 MB
  matched bootstrap files returned: 3
  RESULT: yielding walker keeps the loop responsive — max delay near the 5ms floor,
          98.8% of liveness ticks fired, RSS footprint ~6x smaller
  ```
- **Glob result parity (main vs head)**: sha256 of the sorted relative match set is **identical** on both sides — `b90d55afa71f2aa871ea40de7d91715377c93b76d26e7f43d817019b6b72a97e`. Matched set both sides: `AGENTS.md`, the deep 40-level `deep/.../AGENTS.md`, and `node_modules/pkg000/AGENTS.md`; `.git` and `.hidden/AGENTS.md` correctly excluded by both. The custom walker changes event-loop behavior and memory, not the returned file set.

  | metric (median of 3, 395,807 entries, Node v24.10.0) | main `9b823c610816` | head `3dfd7f1d4952` |
  |---|---:|---:|
  | elapsed (ms) | 834.5 | 1244.8 |
  | max event-loop delay (ms) | 55.5 | 10.7 |
  | mean event-loop delay (ms) | 8.50 | 5.09 |
  | liveness ticks kept | 57.2% | 98.8% |
  | RSS delta (MB) | 358.3 | 57.0 |
  | `**/AGENTS.md` matches returned | 3 | 3 (identical set) |

- **Observed result after fix**: the fix trades a modest wall-clock increase (834ms → 1245ms) for the property the issue actually needs — the event loop stops stalling. Max event-loop delay drops from 55.5ms to 10.7ms (near the 5ms probe floor), liveness-tick retention rises from 57.2% to 98.8%, and peak RSS is ~6x smaller (358MB → 57MB) because the walker no longer buffers the whole `fs.glob` result eagerly. The returned match set is byte-identical (same sha256), so existing `bootstrap-extra-files` configs load the same files. At the field-report scale (much larger real workspaces), `main`'s blocking walk is what produces the 14-22s embedded_run stalls; this benchmark demonstrates the direction and mechanism (blocking `fs.glob` vs cooperative yielding) at 395,807 entries on a single dev box.
- **Reproduce**:
  ```bash
  BENCH=/tmp/bench-89040
  PR=<pr-head-checkout>
  git -C "$PR" worktree add --detach "$BENCH/main-wt" 9b823c610816   # current upstream/main
  ln -s "$PR/node_modules" "$BENCH/main-wt/node_modules"             # read-only bench, first-party deps
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$PR/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  cp "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" "$BENCH/main-wt/bench-bootstrap.mts"
  # build the shared workspace once (reused by both sides, walk mutates nothing)
  (cd "$PR" && node --import tsx/esm "$BENCH/bench-bootstrap.mts" build "$BENCH/ws" 400000)
  # 3 fresh processes per side, run from inside each checkout so the relative import binds
  (cd "$PR"            && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  (cd "$BENCH/main-wt" && node --import tsx/esm --expose-gc ./bench-bootstrap.mts run "$BENCH/ws")
  ```
- **What was not tested**: No full live `embedded_run` with active channel connections was driven end-to-end; this proof exercises the real exported glob-resolution path (`loadExtraBootstrapFilesWithDiagnostics`) and event-loop instrumentation directly rather than through a connected channel. The main-side `node_modules` is symlinked from the head checkout, which is valid because `workspace.ts`'s transitive imports are first-party and the run is read-only. Focused regression coverage lives in `workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts` and `handler.test.ts`.

### Directory-symlink glob parity proof

- **Behavior addressed**: The cooperative walker only descended `Dirent.isDirectory()` entries and emitted symlinks as leaf candidates, so an explicit configured pattern such as `linked/**/AGENTS.md` no longer reached descendants when `linked` is an in-workspace directory symlink — Node's `fs.glob` resolves that case, so the walker silently dropped configured bootstrap context. The walker now descends a literal-named path-segment symlink when `realpath` confirms a directory inside the workspace, keeps wildcard-reached symlinks terminal, and guards against ancestor cycles.
- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout on macOS arm64, Node.js `v24.10.0`. Three regression tests build real temp directories with real `fs.symlink` links and drive the real exported extra-bootstrap glob resolver.
- **Steps run**: `npx vitest run src/agents/workspace.load-extra-bootstrap-files.test.ts src/agents/workspace.test.ts`
- **Observed result**: `Test Files 4 passed (4)`, `Tests 156 passed (156)`. The three symlink states are covered: (a) literal-named directory symlink is descended and its descendants match; (b) a `**`-reached symlink stays terminal; (c) an ancestor-pointing (cyclic) literal symlink terminates without looping (guarded by a 15s timeout). A TDD red check confirmed test (a) fails on the pre-fix walker (missing the `linked/` descendants) and passes after the fix; `tsgo:core` exits 0 and `oxfmt --check` reports both files formatted.
- **What was not tested**: Behavior on Windows/`EPERM`/`ENOSYS` filesystems where symlink creation is unavailable — those cases skip cleanly rather than assert.

Closes #87509

target.title: fix(docker): bound Docker GPG key download with connect timeout
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed and understand the change.

## What Problem This Solves

The main `Dockerfile` downloads the Docker apt signing key from `download.docker.com` with no connect or transfer timeout. A stalled connection during image build could hang indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add `--connect-timeout 10` and `--max-time 120` to the curl invocation at line 295. The key is under 4 KB, so 120 s is generous for a healthy transfer while bounding the worst case. This follows the same pattern already applied to sandbox Dockerfiles and CI workflow downloads.

## User Impact

Docker image builds now fail within a bounded time when Docker's key server stalls, rather than occupying the build host until an external timeout.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/dockerfile.test.ts --run`: 25/25 passed.
- `git diff --check`: passed.
- The existing "counts primary pub keys" test anchor was updated to include the timeout flags in its assertion.

### Real behavior proof (controlled stalled-fetch)

Healthy path — the Docker signing key downloads in under 1 second:

```
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o /tmp/docker.gpg.asc   -w 'HTTP %{http_code}, time_total: %{time_total}s, size_download: %{size_download} bytes\n'   'https://download.docker.com/linux/debian/gpg'
HTTP 200, time_total: 0.690254s, size_download: 3817 bytes
$ file /tmp/docker.gpg.asc
/tmp/docker.gpg.asc: PGP public key block Public-Key (old)
```

Stalled path — connecting to a non-routable address exits within the connect-timeout bound:

```
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 10 -o /dev/null 'https://10.255.255.1:9999/gpg'
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3013 milliseconds
Exit code: 28 (CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT)
Elapsed: 3s (vs >60s without --connect-timeout)
```

Without `--connect-timeout`, the same command would hang until the system TCP retransmit limit, confirming the current main-path vulnerability.
